name: Dreeg (NÃ¼rnberger Dreck)
description: Dreeg (a Franconian dialect form of 'Dreck', meaning trash or muck) is a complex, multiphase card game from the Nuremberg region of Germany. It is a composite game consisting of eight distinct sub-games, all based on the mechanics of Sechsundsechzig (66). Players compete to erase 'strokes' from their slate, and the game is strictly one of elimination: in each phase, players drop out as they succeed, until only one 'loser' remains to face the next challenge.

history.origins: Dreeg is deeply rooted in the Franconian tavern culture of North Bavaria. It evolved as a way to extend the standard game of 66 into a longer, social competition suitable for a 'Stammtisch' (regular's table).
timeline: 1800s: Sechsundsechzig (66) becomes the foundation for many German tavern games.
Early 20th Century: The formal structure of the eight-phase 'Nuremberg Trash' is stabilized.
Modern Era: Maintained by traditional card societies in Nuremberg and Neumarkt.
history.cultural: Typically played with a chalk slate and sponge; losers of individual phases often 'pay' for the round of drinks or local delicacies.
history.evolution: The game incorporates elements of Schafkopf (specifically the Wenz and Solo phases) alongside the core mechanics of 66.

setup.players: Ideally 4 players. Can be played by 3.
setup.deck: 24-card German-suited deck (Bavarian or Franconian pattern). Card ranks: Ace (11), Ten (10), King (4), Ober (3), Unter (2), Nine (0).
setup.dealing: Dealer deals 6 cards to each player (in batches of 3). In some phases, a trump card is turned up; in others, trumps are determined by bidding.
setup.equipment: Deck of cards, chalk slates (Schiefertafeln) for each player, chalk.

rules.objective: Avoid being the last player with strokes left on your slate at the end of each of the eight phases.
rules.gameplay:
The game consists of 8 Phases:
1-2. Einfacher Dreck: Standard 66 play. Players drop out as they reach 66 points in a deal.
3. Hosen Runter: Played with open cards.
4. Scharfer Dreck: Strict 66 with no declarations allowed.
5. Rufer/Bettel: Players bid to win or lose a specific number of tricks.
6-8. Special Phases: Usually includes Solo (a player plays against the rest), Wenz (only Unters are trumps), and a final elimination round.
keyRules: The 'Last Trick' is vital for tiebreaking but does not award points like in standard 66.
Marriages: Declaring King and Ober of the same suit scores 20 (or 40 if trump).
Elimination: In most phases, the last person remaining (who failed to erase their strokes) is the official loser of that phase.

strategy.basic: In the early phases, play defensively to erase your strokes as quickly as possible and drop out before the game becomes 'sharp'.
strategy.intermediate: Counting to 66: Always track the point value of the tricks you have taken. Reaching 66 allows you to 'close' the deck and stop opponents from drawing better cards.
strategy.advanced: Slate Management: Observe how many strokes opponents have left. If a player is on their last stroke, do not feed them high-point cards (Aces/Tens).
tips: The Nine is a 'trash' card with 0 points, but it is excellent for safe leads when you want an opponent to lead a high card.
Use your marriages (King/Ober) early to jumpstart your score toward 66.

variations.name: Stroke notation
variations.description: Some play with Roman III or a crossed seven instead of XII for the seven strokes; first stroke erased differently. Kartl-Akademie Weinzierlein uses 10 strokes (XX) per phase instead of 7.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Notation variant only; no engine parameter changes.

variations.name: Two-player trump indicator
variations.description: In two-player 66 some use the 13th card as trump indicator under the talon; others use the bottom card of the pack turned up and slid under the talon.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Two-player not primary format; overrides to be added if supported.

variations.name: Rot-Assen scoring (Bamberger)
variations.description: Bamberger variant: lone player always erases 3 strokes if successful in Rot-Assen, irrespective of opponents' card points; opponents still erase 1, 2 or 3 if they win.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Regional variant; engine overrides not yet specified.
